stories.title: Payments Manager Corpay Cross-Border Relocates to 18K SF at 560 Lexington Avenue
stories.excerpt: An international payment and currency risk management firm is planning a headquarters relocation to Rudin’s 560 Lexington Avenue. Corpay Cross-Border Solutions, which operates under corporate payments company Corpay, has signed an 11-year lease for 17,778 square feet at the Plaza District tower, Commercial Observer has learned. The landlord declined to provide the asking rent, but an April lease inside Rudin’s 22-story tower asked $84 per square foot, according to previous CO reports. Jacob Rosenthal and Kevin Carroll of CBRE represented Corpay, while Rudin was represented in-house by Kevin Daly and a CBRE team of Peter Turchin, Brett Shannon, Eric Deutsch and Lauren Levy. Corpay Cross-Border plans to move from Tishman Speyer‘s 300 Park Avenue into its new, prebuilt office, which occupies the entire 17th floor of 560 Lexington, this fall. Daly, Rudin’s vice president of office leasing, stated that the deal validates recent portfolio investments, which allowed for minimal modifications to meet Corpay’s space requirements. “This allowed us to accommodate their accelerated timeline for move-in, which was a big factor in getting the deal done,” Daly said. Located two blocks from Grand Central Terminal, the 380,000-square-foot office building at the corner of Lexington Avenue and East 50th Street has seen over 91,000 square feet of leasing activity in the last six months, according to Rudin. Recent arrivals include financial firm Marex, hedge fund SummitTX and coworking firm Industrious. Spokespeople for CBRE and Corpay Cross-Border did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Corpay Cross-Border relocates HQ to 560 Lexington, 17,778 SF, 11-year lease at ~$84/SF
Move from 300 Park Avenue signals tenant confidence in Plaza District office market recovery
Rudin's pre-built space enabled accelerated fall move-in, reducing landlord capex risk
stories.summary: Corpay Cross-Border Solutions signed an 11-year lease for 17,778 square feet at Rudin's 560 Lexington Avenue in Manhattan's Plaza District at approximately $84 per square foot, relocating from Tishman Speyer's 300 Park Avenue. The pre-built, move-in-ready space on the 17th floor accommodated the tenant's accelerated timeline with minimal modifications. The deal validates Rudin's recent portfolio investments and signals selective demand recovery in Midtown Manhattan office.
stories.impact: Office leasing activity in Midtown Manhattan Plaza District supports downtown stabilization and reduces downward rent pressure that would otherwise compress valuation multiples across NYC real estate. However, this is office-focused with limited direct multifamily demand signal; note that office capital redeployment toward residential conversions remains a longer-term play.

stories.title: Charlotte Apartments Trade for $76.3M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer made its first foray into the Charlotte market, purchasing Berkshire Dilworth, a 296-unit luxury multifamily property between West Midtown and the historic Dilworth neighborhood. Berkshire Residential was the seller of the asset, which traded for $76.3 million, or just over $250,000 a unit. Berkshire Dilworth, located at 1351 E. Morehead St., is 97 percent occupied. The unit mix includes studios and one- to three-bedroom floorplans with an average size of 856 square feet. Interior amenities at Berkshire Dilworth comprise a 24-hour fitness center, a yoga studio, a resident lounge, coworking spaces, a clubhouse and a rooftop lounge with a fireplace. Outdoor offerings include a swimming pool, a sundeck and a terrace lounge. The community also includes 3,000 square feet of street-level retail. Tishman Speyer is planning to upgrade the property’s amenities and exterior, along with select apartment improvements. Newmark’s John Heimburger, Dean Smith and Sean Wood represented Berkshire Residential. The post Charlotte Apartments Trade for $76.3M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer acquires Berkshire Dilworth, 296-unit luxury apt, Charlotte for $76.3M ($257K/unit)
97% occupied, 856 SF avg, mixed unit types; includes 3,000 SF retail; property 97% leased
Value-add play: amenity and exterior upgrades planned post-acquisition
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer made its first Charlotte acquisition, purchasing the 296-unit luxury Berkshire Dilworth in West Midtown/Dilworth neighborhood for $76.3 million, or approximately $257,000 per unit. The property is 97% occupied with an average unit size of 856 square feet across studios through three-bedrooms. Tishman Speyer plans selective amenity, exterior, and unit-level upgrades.
stories.impact: Major institutional capital entry into Charlotte multifamily signals market maturation and rent growth confidence in the submarket. Tishman Speyer's acquisition at $257K/unit suggests value-add thesis is still viable; expect downward pressure on Class-B/C land and development pricing as large operators enter and bidding competition intensifies. Demand fundamentals (job growth, in-migration) likely strong enough to justify entry by top-tier operator.

stories.title: Investor Team Pays $91.8M for 2 Charlotte Office Buildings
stories.excerpt: Corebridge Real Estate Investors and Crestlight Capital acquired two buildings in The Station at LoSo mixed-use project in Charlotte. Commercial Search reports that the group paid $91.8 million for the assets, which consist of 200,000 square feet of space. Beacon Partners was the seller. At the time of sale, the buildings were 90 percent leased. JLL’s Ryan Clutter, Mike McDonald, Daniel Flynn and Director CJ Liuzzo led the Capital Markets’ Investment Sales and Advisory team that worked on behalf of Beacon Partners. Located at 3600 and 3700 South Blvd., Station 3 and Station 4 represent the first phase of a roughly 15-acre, master-planned development. Slated to come online in three phases, Beacon Partners’ project also includes MAA LoSo and Ello House, two communities totaling 693 units. Future phases will bring online Station 1 and 2, two additional office buildings set to total roughly 1 million square feet, as well as a 350-unit community expected to break ground this year. The post Investor Team Pays $91.8M for 2 Charlotte Office Buildings appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Corebridge Real Estate & Crestlight Capital buy 2 Charlotte office buildings, Station 3 & 4, $91.8M for 200K SF
Station LoSo mixed-use: 90% leased; phases 1–3 include 693 apt units (MAA LoSo, Ello House) + 350-unit community breaking ground this year
Future phases: 1M+ SF office, making LoSo a major live-work-play hub in Charlotte
stories.summary: Corebridge Real Estate Investors and Crestlight Capital acquired Station 3 and Station 4 office buildings at The Station at LoSo mixed-use development in Charlotte for $91.8 million, totaling 200,000 square feet at 90% occupancy. The roughly 15-acre master-planned project includes 693 existing apartment units (MAA LoSo and Ello House) and is slated to add a 350-unit community breaking ground this year, with future office phases totaling approximately 1 million square feet.
stories.impact: Station LoSo's mixed-use model demonstrates institutional confidence in Charlotte's live-work-play demand; the planned 350-unit phase and additional 1M SF of office create a flywheel of tenant stacking and demand density. This de-risks future multifamily phases and signals sustained rent growth and pre-leasing potential. Developers should monitor LoSo's absorption and phase timing—strong absorption would validate Charlotte's job/population fundamentals and increase land pricing in competing South Boulevard submarket locations.

stories.title: NRP Advancing 312-Unit Port St. Lucie Apartment Venture
stories.excerpt: The NRP Group broke ground on its newest luxury apartment community, a 312-unit development within the 10,000-acre Tradition master-planned community at 13661 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie. M&T Bank provided construction financing. Group 4 Architecture designed the project. This marks The NRP Group’s second development closing in Florida this year. Situated on approximately 18 acres, the development consists of 10, 3-story buildings offering a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom apartment homes ranging from approximately 720 to 1,300 square feet. Every residence will include either a private balcony or a fenced ground-floor yard. Amenities include a 24-hour fitness center with both strength and cardio equipment, a swimming pool, coworking suites and dedicated work-from-home offices, a multipurpose resident lounge with a full kitchen, package concierge and storage facilities, outdoor grilling areas, as well as landscaped courtyards and gathering spaces. Completion is scheduled for summer 2028. The post NRP Advancing 312-Unit Port St. Lucie Apartment Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NRP Group breaks ground on 312-unit luxury apt, Port St. Lucie (Tradition master-plan), M&T Bank financing
18 acres, 10 buildings, 3-story, 720–1,300 SF units; full amenity suite with coworking/work-from-home focus
NRP's second Florida closing in 2025; strong demand signal in 55+ growth corridor
stories.summary: The NRP Group broke ground on a 312-unit luxury apartment community within the 10,000-acre Tradition master-planned community in Port St. Lucie, financed by M&T Bank. The 18-acre development comprises ten 3-story buildings with one-, two-, and three-bedroom units ranging from 720 to 1,300 square feet, including amenities such as fitness, pool, coworking, and dedicated work-from-home offices. This marks NRP's second Florida development close in 2025.
stories.impact: Port St. Lucie's continued buildout signals sustained demand from retirees and remote workers migrating to Florida's lower-cost alternatives to Miami/South Florida. M&T Bank's construction financing appetite confirms market creditworthiness. NRP's repeat capital deployment in Florida this year indicates strong absorption and rent growth expectations; developers should monitor Tradition absorption rates and pricing to calibrate competing West Palm Beach/Port St. Lucie land strategies.

stories.title: John McCullough of Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Development: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Since joining Kennedy Wilson following the firm’s $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers’ apartment living platform in 2025, John McCullough has been serving as president of the real estate investment company’s multifamily development group, where he oversees every aspect of the firm’s U.S. development business. Kennedy Wilson’s acquisition of Toll Brothers’ platform gave it general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties, with assets under management of $2.2 billion. The firm also purchased a pipeline of 29 development sites in various stages of construction. Toll Brothers’ entire apartment living management team has transitioned over to Kennedy Wilson under the leadership of McCullough, who previously led apartment living operations at Toll Brothers. But McCullough’s real estate path wasn’t always laid out for him, as he started out in the U.S. Navy and then eventually hit his business stride at school in Boston. Commercial Observer caught up with McCullough last month to discuss his entry into real estate, the Toll Brothers acquisition, and his mission at Kennedy Wilson. bullets: Kennedy Wilson acquires Toll Brothers apartment platform for $347M (2025); John McCullough named president

stories.summary: Kennedy Wilson acquired Toll Brothers' entire apartment living platform for $347 million, bringing general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties with $2.2 billion in assets under management, plus a pipeline of 29 development sites. stories.impact: This $347M acquisition signals major capital reallocation into multifamily development and operational platforms; Kennedy Wilson's 29-site pipeline creates a meaningful competitive presence across markets. Developers should track which markets and project types Kennedy Wilson prioritizes within its pipeline—this will indicate capital flight away from certain geographies and potential inventory increases in others, affecting land competition and cap rates.

stories.title: Southern Land Company Hires Tony Marchbanks as Head of Homebuilding
stories.excerpt: Southern Land Company has made a leadership hire to spearhead single-family home development in three key states, Commercial Observer has learned. Tony Marchbanks has joined the firm as national president of homebuilding, in which he will focus not only on the U.S., but also focus particularly on Tennessee, Texas and Colorado, according to Southern Land. Marchbanks brings with him 30 years of real estate experience and most recently served as chief operating officer for Highland Homes, where he launched a building spree in the Houston market, producing 1,000 homes per year, Southern Land said. “Higher interest rates and lack of job growth all culminate into a lack of consumer confidence, so you have all three key contributors to a good homebuilding environment that are headwinds at this time,” Marchbanks told CO. “But for a company like Southern Land, it’s actually a huge opportunity because they have expansion plans, particularly into Texas, which is the largest new home market in the country,” Marchbanks said. “Most builders secured their lot supply three years ago, and now they have too many lots. So it’s an opportunity for a company like Southern Land to find and [invest] in communities they wouldn’t have been able to in a strong market.” Southern Land is currently developing four master-planned communities across 5,000 individual lots in its portfolio. Marchbanks will oversee the construction, purchasing, sales and architecture for those soon-to-be neighborhoods. Southern Land has been making some changes in recent months by launching its own mortgage lending division in May to augment its sales division and support its construction pipeline, CO reported at the time. Build-to-sell homes are not the only residential asset class Southern Land has been dabbling in either, as it builds multifamily properties in Las Vegas; Erie, Colo.; and just outside Austin, Tex. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Southern Land Company hires Tony Marchbanks as national president of homebuilding; 30 yrs real estate experience
Focus on Tennessee, Texas, Colorado; Marchbanks launched 1,000 homes/year at Highland Homes (Houston)
Leadership signals expansion in Texas amid higher rates, lack of job growth; lot oversupply creating acquisition opportunity
stories.summary: Southern Land Company appointed Tony Marchbanks as national president of homebuilding, focusing development in Tennessee, Texas, and Colorado. Marchbanks brings 30 years of real estate experience and previously served as COO at Highland Homes, where he launched production of 1,000 homes per year in Houston. He cited higher interest rates, weak job growth, and consumer confidence challenges as headwinds, but identified Texas's largest new-home market status and lot oversupply (from three-year-old purchases) as expansion opportunities.
stories.impact: Marchbanks' hire and Texas focus in a high-rate environment signals Southern Land's confidence in Texas population/migration fundamentals outweighing macro headwinds. Lot oversupply from 2022 purchases creates pricing opportunity for disciplined builders; this suggests land values in Texas may remain depressed longer than in supply-constrained markets, affecting multifamily land competition. Monitor whether single-family builder lot consolidation in Texas compresses multifamily land availability in key metros (Austin, Dallas, Houston).

Baby Boomer wave: first cohort turned 80 in 2016; Harbert capitalized $210M (2016) and $510M (2020) funds
Asset class evolution and investment thesis tied to demographic tailwinds and operational consolidation
stories.summary: Harbert Management Corporation's Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum co-head an $8 billion alternatives asset manager's seniors housing team, which has invested in the space for 15 years. The team raised a $210 million fund in 2016 and a $510 million fund in 2020, and is currently on its third fundraise. stories.title: Sunday Summary: The Rent is Too Damn Low!
stories.excerpt: Back in 2010, Jimmy McMillan ran for governor of New York on a pretty straightforward platform: The rent was too damn high. McMillan said it again and again, and named his political party The Rent is Too Damn High Party. (McMillan’s presence on the debate stage garnered national attention and Matthew Yglesias even titled a slim book with the same name.) Sixteen years later, McMillan is still not wrong, in that the average monthly rent just hit $6,655 in Manhattan according to research from Corcoran Sunshine — which is 10 percent higher than it was a year ago. There are a number of solutions that the Mamdani administration have proffered, but one that has perhaps attracted the most attention has been freezing rents on rent-stabilized apartments. In June, the Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year leases, which will certainly be popular with rent-stabilized voters. But one has to wonder if it will actually address the larger issue of affordability — especially if landlords begin to lose more money than they make on stabilized units. Some landlords are keeping units off the market rather than getting them in rentable shape. “Some of [the rent-stabilized units] require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Jose Tur, who owns two stabilized buildings in Washington Heights and testified before the RGB before their vote. In addition to the baseline, Tur told Commercial Observer that he would probably have to include another $30,000 per unit for the cosmetic fixes. And that’s on the lower end of the renovation spectrum. Matthew Engel, president of Langsam Property Services, says he has units that require $80,000 to $100,000 worth of work, and rent as low as $600 per month. “There’s no way for me to finance that work,” said Engel. “No bank would lend me $100,000 if I’m only going to be able to collect $6,000 a year in rent.”
bullets: Manhattan avg rent hit $6,655/month (Corcoran Sunshine), up 10% YoY; frozen rent-stabilized leases (June) via Rent Guidelines Board
Policy: rent freeze on 1–2 year stabilized leases; uncertainty if landlords lose money on stabilized units long-term
Affordability crisis persists despite freeze; risk of reduced new supply and landlord capital withdrawal
stories.summary: According to Corcoran Sunshine research, Manhattan's average monthly rent reached $6,655, a 10% year-over-year increase. In June, New York's Rent Guidelines Board imposed a freeze on one- and two-year leases for rent-stabilized apartments. The article questions whether the freeze addresses broader affordability issues, particularly if landlords begin losing money on stabilized units and remove them from the market.
stories.impact: Rent stabilization freezes reduce economics on legacy stabilized inventory, creating inventory withdrawal risk and reducing supply-side flexibility. This policy uncertainty pressures new market-rate development as substitution plays; expect compressed value-add opportunities and higher new-construction rents to offset regulatory drag. Developers should avoid new construction in stabilized buildings and focus on market-rate opportunities; watch for landlord pressure to convert or exit stabilized stock, creating potential portfolio sales and rehabilitation opportunities.

stories.title: AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South
stories.excerpt: A new lease with AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park and the expansion and extension of PMG Worldwide’s existing space have been recent highlights at TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Ave. South, which has seen more than 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year. The recent transactions follow K Health’s long-term renewal and the expansion of another TAMI user completed in late 2025. Hanover Park signed a lease for the building’s entire 10th floor, totaling approximately 19,269 square feet. PMG Worldwide renewed its lease on the entire second floor while expanding into the entire third floor, bringing its total footprint to approximately 38,744 square feet. “We’re pleased to welcome Hanover Park to 387 Park Avenue South and to expand our relationship with PMG Worldwide,” said Joe Lanzilotta, Director, Commercial Asset Management at TF Cornerstone. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” The post AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI-native fund administrator) leases entire 10th floor, 19,269 SF at 387 Park Ave. South (Manhattan)
PMG Worldwide renews 2nd floor, expands to 3rd floor; 38,744 SF total; 100K+ SF leased in past year
TAMI tenant attraction and expansion signal sustained demand for office in South Park Avenue corridor
stories.summary: AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park signed a lease for the entire 10th floor (19,269 square feet) at TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in Manhattan. PMG Worldwide renewed its second-floor lease and expanded into the entire third floor, bringing its total footprint to 38,744 square feet. The property has logged more than 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year, following renewals and expansions by K Health and other TAMI users.
stories.impact: This is office-focused with limited direct multifamily demand signal; however, the 100K+ SF of leasing activity and TAMI tenant (high wage earner) concentration in South Park Avenue indicates sustained office demand recovery in Manhattan south of traditional Midtown, which could support nearby residential demand and rent growth in East Village/Gramercy submarkets. Office anchoring may stabilize Class-B residential asset values nearby.

stories.title: PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital
stories.excerpt: PMB, a leading healthcare real estate developer, and Loma Linda University Health with Lifepoint Rehabilitation, a business unit of Lifepoint Health, recently broke ground on a new, 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands. Located at 11207 New Jersey., the three-story facility will function as a standalone hospital. “Breaking ground today represents far more than just laying the foundation for a new building – it’s a promise to the community,” said Nolan Weinberg, SVP of Development for PMB. “Inpatient rehabilitation is a critical bridge between acute medical recovery and returning to everyday life..” Loma Linda University Rehabilitation Hospital will be jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation. A summer 2028 opening is expected. Upon completion, Loma Linda University Health will transition its existing inpatient rehabilitation unit to the new facility. PMB’s partners on the project include general contractor Layton Construction, architect Material Design Architects and financing partner Harrison Street Asset Management. The post PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PMB & Loma Linda University Health break ground on 80-bed inpatient rehab hospital, Redlands (San Bernardino County), 99K SF
Harrison Street Asset Management financing; Layton Construction GC; summer 2028 opening; Loma Linda transitions existing rehab unit
Healthcare real estate development in Inland Empire; signals institutional capital in medical facility expansion
stories.summary: PMB and Loma Linda University Health broke ground on a 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands (San Bernardino County), financed by Harrison Street Asset Management. The three-story standalone facility will be jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation and is expected to open in summer 2028. Upon completion, Loma Linda will transition its existing inpatient rehabilitation unit to the new facility.
stories.impact: This is healthcare real estate, not multifamily; limited direct relevance. However, institutional healthcare capital investment in the Inland Empire (San Bernardino County) signals population stability and institutional demand in markets that multifamily developers may target. Monitor whether healthcare facility anchors (hospitals, rehab centers) attract ancillary multifamily demand via employee in-migration and job clustering.
